questions.prompt:
Which of the following principles of divine morality does this verse refer to?
والله بما تعملون بصير
questions.topic: Foundations of divine morality and divine supervision
questions.note: Within the course's framework, the verse describes God seeing what people do: divine supervision. First-term Lesson 1 distinguishes this from revelation, resurrection and satisfaction. The review's apple case illustrates the same principle of being unable to hide from God (p. 9), but is not a quotation of this exam verse.

questions.prompt: For which one is command ethics appropriate?
questions.topic: Types and teaching methods of ethical research
questions.note: The supplied first-term notes assign commanding-and-forbidding ethics to adolescents (up to fifteen), descriptive ethics to young children, and meta-ethics to young people and adults. This is the course's pedagogical classification, not a universal developmental rule. It is absent from the current review PDF; consult the lesson notes pp. 4–5.

questions.prompt: According to the divine word, when does man have the power to distinguish right from wrong?
options: When he/she is a good student
questions.note: In the notes' religious account, piety restores purity and supports discernment. Merely holding the role of scientist, teacher or student is not the condition asked for. This is a course-specific theological claim; it does not imply that nonreligious people cannot learn. The current review does not reproduce the full piety-and-knowledge lesson.

questions.prompt: In which ethical research do we use the method of logical coercion?
questions.topic: Types and teaching methods of ethical research
questions.note: Lesson 2 explicitly calls the method of commanding-and-forbidding ethics 'logical coercion'. Descriptive ethics uses historical/narrative accounts; meta-ethics examines ethical concepts. The terminology is retained from the source. This topic is missing from the current review PDF.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of putting piety next to science?
options: You will be given the power to distinguish right from wrong.
Piety returns the human soul to its original purity and honesty.
questions.note: The green source mark is D, but first-term Lesson 3, question 4 explicitly says that linking piety with knowledge does NOT mean ungodly people cannot learn. Thus A is false within these notes and D cannot stand. C directly reproduces the stated explanation. B is also compatible with the lesson's account of discernment, so both B and C are accepted for this imprecise stem. This correction is an editorial study judgment, not an official replacement key.

questions.prompt: Which one is NOT true about the knowledge of ethics (science of Akhlaq)?
options: It identified good and bad behaviors
In the knowledge of ethics we study Khulq and Khalq
It studies good and bad action
It deals with human characteristics traits like vices and virtues
questions.topic: Khulq, khalq and the scope of ethics
questions.note: Lesson 2 distinguishes acquired moral character (khulq) from bodily creation (khalq). Its definition of moral knowledge concerns moral traits, virtues, vices and related actions, not bodily creation as such. B is the intended exception under that definition. The current review PDF does not contain this definitions lesson.

questions.prompt: Based on the Islam, which one is NOT allowed in searching for knowledge?
options: Seek the knowledge in people of hypocrisy (disunion)
questions.topic: Seeking knowledge without time or place restrictions
questions.note: D retains the supplied study mark. Lesson 3 pp. 6–7 supports seeking beneficial knowledge without time/place restrictions. For C, supplementary primary-text support is Nahjul Balagha, sayings 79–80, which permits taking wisdom even from a hypocrite. That external reference corroborates the principle; it is not proof of this paper's course level or an official exam key. The negatively worded stem uses D as 'none of A–C is prohibited'.

questions.prompt: Which meaning is more complete about moderation?
options: Moderation in any task should be done to the extent that it does not interfere with other tasks
Eating a little - do not walk fast - sleep less.
Do not treat everyone the same.
questions.topic: Moderation and balance between faculties and duties
questions.note: A best captures the lesson's broad balance between responsibilities. Lesson 4 gives moderation in worship alongside proper management of daily life; moderation is not simply minimising food, walking or sleep. The full moderation lesson is not in the current review; a planning reference would not substitute for it.

questions.prompt: According to Aristotle when do we reach bravery?
options: If someone achieves balance with respect to their faculty of reasoning
If someone achieves balance with respect to their faculty of anger
If someone achieves balance with respect to their faculty of appetite
questions.topic: Moderation and balance between faculties and duties
questions.note: The Aristotelian classification taught in Lesson 4 maps balanced reasoning to wisdom, balanced anger to bravery, and balanced appetite to modesty. Therefore B, not the reasoning or appetite options. This distinction is absent from the current review PDF.

questions.prompt: When do problems start in our life?
options: When we commit a small sin
When we do not tell our problems to others
questions.topic: Moderation and balance between faculties and duties
questions.note: In this moderation-lesson context, the source's intended answer is B: imbalance between faculties and duties. This is not a claim that every real-life difficulty is caused by personal imbalance. Lesson 4 contrasts the balanced mean with excess or deficiency; the current review does not include this complete lesson.
